titre: Guido of Arezzo Did More Than Invent Do, Re, Mi
accroche: Around 1025, a Benedictine monk devises a method so that a cantor can read, without ever having heard it, an unknown chant.
contenu_vulgarise:
Around 1025, at the cathedral school of Arezzo, in Tuscany, Bishop Tedald entrusts a young Benedictine monk, Guido, with the training of cantors. The method in use is purely oral: a novice learns the liturgical repertoire by listening to a master repeat it, year after year, until he retains it by heart. Neumes, the only written signs available, indicate that a note goes up or down, never by how much: they recall a melody already known, they do not allow one to learn a new one.

Guido takes on this lock. He starts from an 8th-century hymn dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, *Ut queant laxis*, attributed to the Lombard monk Paul the Deacon. By a coincidence that Guido exploits rather than creates, each of the first six phrases of the melody begins one note higher than the one before. In singing the hymn, one therefore sings, without knowing it, the first six degrees of a scale. Guido takes the first syllable of each phrase, ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, and makes them the names of the notes: the first Western solfège method.

## What the letter on an unknown chant really solves

The real problem Guido is trying to solve is how to transmit a chant that no one has yet sung in front of the student. His best-known treatise, written around 1028 as a letter to a monk of Pomposa, is titled *Epistola de ignoto cantu*, literally “the letter on an unknown chant.” To achieve this, Guido perfects a staff system: horizontal lines, two of which are marked with a color to locate reference notes, on and between which the neumes are placed. The exact pitch of a note is now read from its position, no longer from the memory one keeps of it. A cantor who can read the staff can, in theory, decipher a tune he has never heard.

## What it shifts

History has mostly retained from Guido a pedagogical ditty, do-re-mi, easier to tell than a four-line staff. But the names of the notes change nothing about what one can do with them: what really shifts musical practice in the 11th century is the staff, because it makes music legible independently of memory and of the presence of a master who already knows it. Purely oral transmission, which limited the repertoire to what a cantor could retain, gives way to a text that can be read at a distance, in time as in space: the condition, centuries later, for a score to travel without its composer.

repere.texte: The very title of Guido's most famous treatise, written around 1028, announces it: Epistola de ignoto cantu, “letter on an unknown chant.” Its aim is not to make listening easier but to let a cantor decipher on his own a melody he has never heard, thanks to a staff with colored reference lines that fixes the exact pitch of each note.

carte.punch: Do, re, mi was not the goal. Guido wanted people to read a chant never heard.
carte.idee: Around 1025, the monk Guido of Arezzo draws from the chant Ut queant laxis the syllables ut-re-mi-fa-sol-la. But his real goal lies elsewhere: a staff with reference lines that lets a cantor decipher, alone, a melody never heard, the very subject of his treatise Epistola de ignoto cantu.

quiz.question: What is Guido of Arezzo's Epistola de ignoto cantu really trying to solve?
choix: Giving a memorable, easy-to-remember name to the seven notes of the musical scale
Letting a cantor decipher an unknown chant thanks to a staff that fixes the pitch of each note
Replacing the existing neumes with a notation that also indicates rhythm precisely
Standardizing the liturgical melodies sung in the different abbeys of Europe
quiz.explication: The very title of the treatise, “letter on an unknown chant,” says it: Guido is not only seeking to name the notes but to make a melody legible without ever having heard it, thanks to a staff with lines that fixes the exact pitch. Neumes already served to note the melodic contour and the rhythm, and liturgical standardization is not the subject of the treatise: naming the notes is only a means, not the end pursued.
